# Handover — three-session portaBaltica run, 2026-09-03

> **What this file is.** A dated record of one multi-session run, committed here because the run
> ledger lived in a session-scoped SQLite database that dies with the session — and because a
> session-state `files/` directory is keyed to *one* session and is not reachable by the next one.
> Measured at the time of writing: **272 session-state directories on this machine, 77 of them
> holding artefacts nobody can find.** This one is in the repo so it can be found.
>
> **It is not a book.** `AGENTS.md`, `PROGRAMME.md` and `DESIGN.md` are the books and they grow.
> This is dated, closed, and will not be extended — so it carries no line ceiling, unlike the
> proposal in section E.
>
> **Status at commit time.** Section B is **shipped** (#392). Section A (7 `AGENTS.md` items),
> section C (4 portaBaltica items) and section D (3 `mySkills` items) were **open**, and the books
> were locked to a single writer during the run, which is why they were routed rather than
> written. Check each against master before acting — several were true when written and this file
> carries no guard that keeps them true.
>
> **Written by:** the orchestrating session of that run, 2026-09-03, after all three writer
> sessions had stood down. Recorded here because every session pushes as one GitHub login, so no
> metadata field can say who wrote what — see the artefact rules in section F.

Every item below was **measured**, not intended, and carries the command that
reproduces it. Nothing here is a to-do someone invented at the end.

**Run:** 3 concurrent writer sessions, 06:12Z–09:12Z, orchestrated from this session.
**Shipped:** 8 pull requests, all merged, 0 WIP, 0 no-ops. Tests 2796 → 2815.

```
KEY: authored, by branch
  newsroom  #387 #388 #391 #392   4
  data      #390 #393 #395        3
  UI        #389                  1
KEY: verified but not authored
  newsroom verified #393 · UI verified #392
CONTROL  gh pr view 99999 -> "Could not resolve"   the probe can say no
```

⚠️ **Those keys are here because I got them wrong in my own closing summary** — I wrote "three
PRs" for a session that authored four, and "three self-corrections" for one that made six. Both
figures were right under a key I never stated (PLAN 1 PRs; corrections to figures already sent).
The run's single most repeated finding, arriving in the summary that closes it, from the person
who spent the day asking everyone else for denominators.

**Filed:** issue #394 (infrastructure, `what-if` confirmed).

⚠️ **Attribution, corrected on the session's own account.** The contradiction in `main.bicep`
(L202 `allowBlobPublicAccess: false` against L252 `publicAccess: 'Blob'`) was spotted by the
**newsroom session**, *"while looking for something else, in a file I was not allowed to touch."*
I confirmed it with `az deployment group what-if` and filed it. Joint finding, and the session
found it first.

**That is the write-boundary effect producing the run's one finding with production
consequences** — a redeploy of `main.bicep` as written would have taken the news site down, and
`what-if` reports the change with **no error**:

```
allowBlobPublicAccess      true -> false
articles.publicAccess    "Blob" -> "None"
```

A session that could not edit the file read it instead. See the write-boundary entry in F.

**Scorecard:** `Verification` — ⚠️ **two axes, and I published them as one line.** Measured:

```
        comments   posted        merged        ordering
#392        1      08:52:53Z     07:56:02Z     57 min AFTER    ❌
#393        1      08:07:41Z     08:13:10Z     5.5 min BEFORE  ✅
                                               reviews 0 on both
CONTROL  PR 99999 -> "Could not resolve"   the probe can say no
```

⚠️ **THE COUNT IS IDENTICAL AND THE ORDERING IS OPPOSITE.** Both PRs carry exactly one comment,
3298 and 4942 chars, same author, `reviews: 0` on both. **A count-based discriminator reports both
as verified.** Only the timestamp comparison separates them — which is this run's own central
finding (*two states, one artefact*) arriving in the instrument built to measure it.

⚠️ **And I corrected the reviewer wrongly on this — their `#392 comments 0` was CORRECT when
taken.** They flagged their own claim as unmeasured and asked me to check rather than accept it.
Measured:

```
#392 comment  created 08:52:53Z  3298 chars
  opens: "**Post-merge verification (Track 1, UI session).** Recorded here because this PR
          merged with `reviews: 0` and `comments: 0` ..."

so at their reading (~08:17Z) the count WAS 0; Track 1 posted at 08:52:53Z
```

**The comment documents the very state they reported**, and it is not theirs. So their figure was
a **premise that expired in transit**, not a misreading — the run's eighth instance of *true when
written, false when read*, and **the first inside a scorecard rather than a message.** That is the
worse venue: a scorecard is read long after anyone who could date it has gone.

⚠️ **And the author field cannot help.** Both comments read `samoletovs`, because every session
pushes as one login — the same structural fact that makes `reviews: 0` unreachable. **Only the
content discriminates**, which is why an artefact must name its own author and its own timing in
its opening lines. Track 1's does, in its first sentence, unprompted.

⚠️ **Scored on both artefacts, and the reviewer's own fails it — measured on their insistence:**

```
                  names WHO / track   names TIMING
#392  Track 1           True              True
#393  Track 3           False             True
CONTROL  impossible string in either artefact : False
```

Track 1 opens *"Post-merge verification (Track 1, UI session). Recorded here because this PR
merged with `reviews: 0` and `comments: 0`…"* — who, which track, and when relative to the merge,
in one sentence. Track 3 opens with the **finding** — *"Verified — and the PR's central claim is
incomplete…"* — a defensible choice that still omits the one thing no field can supply.

**Track 1 wrote it that way because it knew no field would carry it.** That is the version to
standardise: the third property of a working artefact, after *readable* and *actionable without a
round trip*, is **self-dating and self-attributing**.

⚠️ **And the reviewer's correction to the unmeasured-flag rule is better than mine.** I wrote that
a claim marked unmeasured *"cannot mislead"*; they pointed out that undersells its real cost —
**it moves the work to the reader**:

> **An unmeasured claim without its discriminating command is just a hedge; with one, it is a
> handoff. The command is the whole difference.**

That is what made their `#392 comments 0` flag work: they attached the command that settles it, so
the cost to me was one line and bounded. Without it the same sentence is an escape hatch.

That corrects a proposal made at the close: a session suggested `comments` as the discriminator
`reviews` could never be. It is not. The discriminator is **`comment.createdAt < mergedAt`**, and it
is a comparison rather than a count — **plus a timestamp on the reading itself**, without which
even the right comparison describes a moment that has passed.

- **Artefact ✅ on both** — the reconciliations exist, are public, and state their own limitations.
- **Ordering ❌ on #392, ✅ on #393** — one documented, one gated.

**#393 is the demonstration that the rule is workable, not merely desirable.** Track 1 proposed
*"post the reconciliation before merging, so the artefact and the gate are one object"*; #393 was
already doing it, 5.5 minutes ahead of its own merge, by a different session. The rule was
practised before it was written down.

**Both attributions in the record were partial.** I wrote *"a plan defect, not a session failure"*;
the session wrote *"I merged on a standing authorisation while a specific instruction was in
flight."* Both true, neither whole: PLAN 2 required no ordering, **and** a standing authorisation
silently outranked a specific instruction still in transit — the run's own *every crossed message
resolved to a default* finding, inside the gate meant to prevent it. A verifier who cannot block a
merge is a reviewer. See D1.

**Keeping the red rather than reverting** — the session's argument and it is right: *a revert buys
a clean history and destroys the one artefact that makes the lesson stick.*

## A. portaBaltica — `AGENTS.md`

### A1. `[datetime]::Parse` — the entry is wrong twice over ⚠️ REPLACE

The file records that `[datetime]::Parse` on a `ConvertFrom-Json` value **throws**. Measured
on `en-150`, ground truth `2026-09-03T04:55:05Z`:

```
[string]$v        09/03/2026 04:55:05   INVARIANT (MM/dd)
"$v"              09/03/2026 04:55:05   INVARIANT   (interpolation IS [string])
$v.ToString()     03/09/2026 04:55:05   CURRENT culture (dd/MM)
$v.ToString('o')  2026-09-03T04:55:05.0000000Z

input                1-arg          3-arg inv+utc
the OBJECT           2026-03-09 ✗   2026-09-03 ✓
[string]$v           2026-03-09 ✗   2026-09-03 ✓
"$v"                 2026-03-09 ✗   2026-09-03 ✓
$v.ToString()        2026-09-03 ✓   2026-03-09 ✗    <- INVERTS
$v.ToString('o')     2026-09-03 ✓   2026-09-03 ✓    <- safe in BOTH
```

**Mechanism:** the culture that *stringifies* must match the culture that *parses*.

**Two corrections, not one.** It does **not** always throw — it silently returns 9 March
for 3 September. And that may be **locale-dependent**: on a `MM/dd` host the same coercion
gives an out-of-range day for some dates and genuinely throws, so the entry is *true on some
hosts and dangerously false on others*.

**Reconciles to the unit:** `2026-09-03 − 2026-03-09 = 178 days`, exactly the absurd age one
session had flagged and disbelieved hours before either of us knew why.

**Rule:** do not round-trip through a string; if you must, `ToString('o')`.

⚠️ Two people independently converged on a *wrong shared mechanism* ("object vs stringify")
because neither stated **which** stringification they used. Credit the disagreement.

### A2. `mergeStateStatus: UNSTABLE` is two states under one field ⚠️ REPLACE

The file says it means a required check is **failing**. It also means **not yet finished**.
Both of this run's PRs sat `UNSTABLE` while entirely green-in-progress; #393 read `UNSTABLE`
with 0 failing and 1 queued.

**Discriminating read:** `gh pr checks <n>` separates `pending` from `fail`.
`mergeStateStatus` cannot. (The file is already right that `mergeable` answers a different
question.)

### A3. `npm ci` proxy failure — and the check that certifies it is worthless ADD

```
E404 GET .../react-router-dom-7.18.3.tgz     the corporate proxy, not the branch
GET 7.18.2 -> 200 (2382 bytes)   POSITIVE CONTROL
GET 7.18.3 -> 404
HEAD both  -> 405                a HEAD probe cannot distinguish them at all
```

⚠️ **Do not verify a copied `node_modules` by hash-comparing `package-lock.json`.** That check
**passes while what it establishes is false** — and it fails in the *reassuring* direction: it
passes most confidently when both trees are stale in the same way, which is the case it was
introduced to exclude. The discriminating read is the installed version in
`node_modules/<pkg>/package.json`. Root cause: the proxy has no 7.18.3 at all, so **no tree
here can satisfy the lock**.

Also: `$env:GIT_ROOT` is unset, so `cd $env:GIT_ROOT` silently lands in the home directory and
repo-relative scripts report `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` — which reads as "the script is missing".

### A4. Application Insights returns a confident zero ADD

`portabaltica-ai` is **workspace-based**, so `az monitor app-insights query` reports `n=0 EVER`
on a correctly configured component. **Two changes are needed together** — the log-analytics
workspace endpoint **and** the table `AppTraces` rather than `traces`. Either alone still
returns zero. Fails toward "nothing here".

### A5. `Tee-Object | Select-Object -Last N` buffers ADD

A running suite looks hung. Measured: with `-Last 2` both lines land at 2244/2245ms; without
it, 118/807/1519ms progressive. It buffers **by construction** — it cannot know the last N
until the stream ends. Read the tee'd file directly.

### A6. The plant's applied-check must match the plant's **shape** ADD

Existing rules ("anchor exactly once", "read the applied-flag before the pass count") silently
assume a **substitution**. For an **insertion** the anchor stays in place by design, so
"the original clause is gone" reads `False` on a plant that *did* apply. Insertion-shaped
check: new content present exactly once, anchor still present, phantom absent beforehand.

### A7. A tense doing work the measurement cannot support CONSIDER — probably leave alone

Item 4 says the main checkout's `node_modules` "is empty", present tense. It was **non-empty**
at 09:16 and empty at 09:33; a failed `npm ci` deletes before installing. Both readings honest,
the entry correct as written — and it means the original copy advice was **viable when given**.
The instruction ("do not reach for it without looking") is robust either way.

## C. portaBaltica — open work

### C1. No standing guard on `CHECK_STATUS` ⚠️ OPEN

```
files mentioning CHECK_STATUS : scripts/source-alert.mjs   (only)
...of which under tests/      : NONE
CONTROL tests mentioning system-status       : 14
CONTROL tests mentioning an impossible token :  0
```

The **value** was fixed (`pending` is in the set); the **guard** never was, so producer and
consumer can drift again silently. `AGENTS.md` says why it must be **static**: the `pending`
state fires on a timing condition — measured at `759ms` against a `750ms` optional budget, a
9ms overrun, at roughly 6% of requests — so a live test passes ~94% of runs while testing
nothing.

### C2. `power-prices.zones[].tomorrow` — an opportunity, needs a start after 11:00Z DEFERRED

Computed, serialised, and read by **zero code** in `src/` (comments stripped block-first then
line: `raw=1 CODE=0`, the single raw hit being a comment). Three positive controls fire, negative
control silent. The card draws a day-boundary line and prints an interval count and never shows
tomorrow's prices, while the producer's own docstring calls it *"the only genuinely
forward-looking number on the dashboard"*.

⚠️ **Start after 11:00Z.** Before Nord Pool publishes, `tomorrow` is null for all four zones and a
live probe cannot separate "the UI drops it" from "there is none to drop". It is also a **design
decision** — twelve numbers at 320px on a card that already carries a series, a boundary line and
a count — not a wiring fix.

### C3. Rejection counts for tier B/C AUTHORISED, stopped by budget

Counts **and check names only** — never a slug, never a snippet. Slugs derive from third-party
headlines and `runs/` is publicly readable, so they stay escalated.

```python
for card in report.syndicated where status == 'rejected':
    for c in card.provenance['validator']['checks'] where not c['passed']:
        counts[c['name']] += 1
```

Never touches `RunReport.rejected`, so **no slug can leak by construction** rather than by
someone remembering. Leak vector checked: `CheckResult.detail` for `snippet_verbatim` reports
byte lengths and an offset, never the text. ~15 lines plus a test and a plant.

### C4. `api/shared/ecb.js` docstring — SHIPPED as #395

Recorded because the reasoning matters: the docstring credited the whole fix to the parser
unification. One parser removes **vocabulary** drift; the `rates.length === 0` throw removes
**field** drift, because `freshness` reads `referenceDate` while the ticker reads `rates`. A
future reader tidying away the "redundant" throw would have silently reopened the gap.

## D. `mySkills` — the multi-agent skill

Two commits: `f6fc177` (on origin) and **`33c35fc` — committed, rebased, NOT pushed**.
`ahead 1`, clean tree, no conflicts. Push is the one action deliberately not taken: it is
irreversible and the owner was unavailable.

### D1. Verifier artefact — **ordering** STRENGTHEN

Shipped: *"the verifier must leave a readable artefact."* Better, and it closes the hole that
produced the rule: **post the reconciliation as a PR comment *before* merging**, so the artefact
and the gate are the same object. Makes the ordering failure impossible rather than merely
visible.

⚠️ Load-bearing constraint: `gh pr review --approve` **fails for every session** here — all push
as one login, so GitHub refuses ("Can not approve your own pull request"). **A comment is the
only artefact the mechanism permits**, so `reviews: 0` can never be evidence of an unverified PR.

⚠️ **STATUS CHANGE — this rule is no longer reasoned, it is demonstrated.** It was added to gate 3
on my noticing that my own PLAN named a verifier without requiring an artefact. It is now backed
by a run of the mechanism end to end, between two sessions that never spoke to each other:

```
#393   reviews 0 · comments 1        the comment was the ENTIRE channel
       the newsroom session reviewed the data session's PR and left its
       finding, with the measurement it re-ran, as a comment
#395   title "One parser removes vocabulary drift; the throw removes field drift"
       = the review's recommendation, shipped by the PR's own author
```

Verified independently on master with a positive control: the over-claim `'at any strictness'` is
gone, the `NOT sufficient` warning is present, the `rates`-empty throw survives, `parseDaily` ×5 in
a 4553-byte file proves the probe reads, impossible string `False`.

**A comment naming what was re-run and what it printed was readable enough for a stranger to act
on, and it outlived the session that wrote it.** Testimony in chat would have died at 09:00Z. This
is the strongest single argument in the run for gate 3, and it required no enforcement from me.

### D2. A verified SHA is not the merged SHA ADD

⚠️ **The shape, which is more useful than the instance: two opposite failures sit under one check,
and it sees one of them.**

```
STALE RECORD      the PR record lags behind the branch      the check CATCHES it   (#146/#311)
ADVANCING BRANCH  the branch moves after the read           the check is BLIND
                  -> both produce the same passing reading
```

The check was endorsed *because* it caught the first, which is exactly what stopped anyone asking
whether it covered the second. Same taxonomy as everything else this run found — two states, one
artefact — arriving in a **guard** rather than in a probe.

The standing check compares the **PR record** against `ls-remote`. Observed: verified `1f17867`,
merged `084fc4a3`.

**Discriminating read:** `git diff <verified>..<merged>` scoped to **production** files, with a
control file expected to differ — four "identical" readings are otherwise equally consistent with
a broken comparison. **A clean result from an untested instrument is the thing this programme
spends its time on**, and it nearly landed here.


### D3. Open in `LESSONS.md`

`mechanism:` is dropped from PLAN BLOCKs — present in 1 of 3 plans in v7 and 0 of 2 in v8, after
being encoded in Step 1b, the template **and** gate check 2. Prescribed escalation: its own
numbered gate item. `SKILL.md` is at exactly **500/500**, so it must be paid for, and the protocol

## E. A finding about the books themselves

`portaBaltica`'s books have **no executed line ceiling** and the skill does. Same afternoon, same
orchestrator:

```
mySkills      SKILL.md  500 -> 500    five rules added, six sections compressed to pay
              LESSONS   500 -> 421    18 settled lessons archived out
portaBaltica  AGENTS    6722 -> 6835  +113 -0    nothing removed
              PROGRAMME 2800 -> 2856   +84 -28   28 lines WERE removed
```

⚠️ **The right-hand column is a correction to this section and to its author's own self-criticism,
and it runs in their favour.** The session wrote *"I added 169 lines and removed nothing."* `169` is
the **net** of #392 (`+197 -28`); the gross is 197 and the removals are real. So *"nothing removed"*
is true of `AGENTS.md` and **false of `PROGRAMME.md`**.

⚠️ **And it is worse than a net-versus-gross confusion — they had printed the `-28` themselves, in
the same message.** Their own numstat at 08:04Z carried `+84 28 PROGRAMME.md` four lines above the
sentence that denied it. So it was a **reading error on data already in hand**, in the direction of
self-accusation.

> **A wrong reading defends itself when it is a self-criticism, because nobody audits one.**

That is the run's central shape with the sign flipped, and it is the reason the audit was worth
running: **a correction nobody looks for is one that makes someone else look better.** Every
incentive ran the other way — they had conceded it, I had published it, agreeing was free.

⚠️ **Their refinement is sharper than the credit, and it is the conclusion this section should
carry:**

```
AGENTS.md      +113   -0    the work was ADDITION      -> no deletion happened
PROGRAMME.md    +84  -28    the work was REPLACEMENT   -> deletion was intrinsic
```

**The discipline appeared where the task shape demanded it, not where it was chosen.** Three
`PROGRAMME.md` items were corrections to existing text, so removal came free with the work; the
`AGENTS.md` items were new sections, and nothing removed anything. That is a narrower virtue than
*"deleted without a gate"* — and **the gap is exactly where a ceiling would have bitten.**

So section E's conclusion is not *"one party had discipline and the other had a machine."* It is:
**a ceiling is only load-bearing for pure addition, which is precisely the case where no other
force removes anything.** Replacement polices itself.

The difference is not discipline — it is that one file has a ceiling **with a check** and the
other does not. A ratio is argued about after the fact; a ceiling is read now.

⚠️ **The `109` was NOT mine — attribution corrected on the reviewer's own insistence, against
their interest.** It came from their 08:04Z message, and their stated command **reproduces
exactly on master**:

```
git grep -n "AGENTS\.md" origin/master -- tests newsroom/tests scripts   -> 109
the same command on MY working tree                                      -> 107
my HEAD affe582 · origin/master a5d2eaf · behind by 8 commits
CONTROL  impossible pattern, same key, same tree                         ->   0
POSITIVE their needle, same key, same tree                               -> 109
```

So I disputed a correct figure from a **stale worktree** — the third instance of that trap in a
single exchange, and it produced a false correction rather than a false finding.

**Their point is sharper than the attribution:** their key was stated as *"across `tests/` and
`scripts/`"*, which names two of three directories and no file types. **Partially keyed reads as
keyed**, and that is worse than stating no key at all — a reader checks the two directories you
named, gets a different number, and cannot tell whether you were wrong or they were. Exactly what
happened here.

⚠️ **And the command that produced my wrong reading had a control that never ran.**
`Write-Host "...{0}" -f $x` does not format: `-f` binds to **`ForegroundColor`**. The count was
`0`, and `[ConsoleColor]0` is **`Black`** — a valid colour — so it bound silently, printed the
literal `{0}`, and exited 0.

```
count 0   -> valid ConsoleColor (Black) -> binds, prints "{0}", exit 0   SILENT
count 42  -> invalid              -> throws, exit 1                      LOUD
[enum]::IsDefined([ConsoleColor], 0)  = True
[enum]::IsDefined([ConsoleColor], 42) = False
```

**The failure is specific to the passing case.** A control returning its expected `0` corrupts
the instrument silently; any other value would have errored. So the one reading a control exists
to produce is the one that disables it — and in a repo whose whole subject is controls, that is
the sharpest instance of *two states, one artefact* the run produced. Use the format operator on
a string (`"...{0}" -f $x`), never `Write-Host ... -f`.

⚠️ **The reviewer's reformulation is the property rather than the bug, and it inverts this
book's own remedy:**

> **The instrument breaks only when its answer is unsurprising.**

A negative control returning `0` is *what you went looking for*. So this is not merely a check
that can fail to fail — its failure is **conditioned on the one reading you were least likely to
question.** The taxonomy above says an absurd reading defends itself and a plausible one does
not; here the reading is neither absurd nor merely plausible, it is **expected**, and the
standing advice — *be suspicious of surprising readings* — points exactly the wrong way.

The remedy is therefore structural rather than vigilant: **make the control's own execution
observable**, by printing it through a path that cannot silently bind, or by running the positive
control in the same command so a dead instrument shows two wrong answers instead of one right-
looking one.

Three honest keys over `origin/master`, three different numbers:

```
KEY A  tests+scripts, .ts/.tsx/.mjs/.js       58 mentions
KEY B  all code+config, incl .py/.yml        138 mentions
my earlier figure, key never stated          109

files that actually READ either book, under EVERY key   0
CONTROL  readFileSync across tests/           177   <- the probe finds it elsewhere
```

**Read the zero, not the totals.** Every denominator moves with the key; the zero does not, and the
control proves the probe can find `readFileSync` when it is there. That is this repo's own rule
arriving in the measurement of its own books — and the unkeyed `109` is mine, not a session's.

**The sharper half, stated in the direction I had not:** *nothing would catch a book that had
rotted.* **No gate can move, and no gate can complain.** A ceiling makes growth visible; zero
readers makes *wrongness* invisible. They are different defects and the second is the worse one —
`AGENTS.md` has already carried a false example, a locale-dependent claim, and a recommendation
(`--diff-filter=D`) that returns a confident zero, and each was found by a person reading it, never
by a check.

Blast radius: **0 readers** under every key. No gate parses either book.

## F. What the run measured about the method

⚠️ **The last instance was in a shell, not in anything anyone was measuring — and it is the run's
own thesis arriving in the test harness.**

A session ran the suite from a worktree it had not confirmed. The hazard was never the exit code
or the empty output:

> **A clean `2815 passed` about the wrong tree is indistinguishable from a clean `2815 passed`
> about the right one.**

It had a tell only because the command printed *nothing* and the session stopped to ask why. **Had
it printed the number expected, it would have been reported — wrong, and with evidence.**

Two environment traps behind it, both silent:

```
$env:GIT_ROOT     UNSET -> `cd $env:GIT_ROOT` lands in the HOME directory, exit 0
Set-Location      moves PowerShell's cwd but NOT [Environment]::CurrentDirectory,
                  so .NET file APIs keep writing to the previous worktree
```

**The verdict worth carrying, in the actionable form:** *the expensive instrument was sound and the
cheap ones were not.* Every heavyweight gate this run relied on — the suites, `what-if`, the live
probes, CI — told the truth. The failures were in one-line shells, remembered needles, unkeyed
counts and unmeasured line numbers. **That says where to look next time**, which the descriptive
version does not.

⚠️ **The last line of this run was an unmeasured number inside a fenced block, and it was mine.**
Closing out, I wrote `передача 500 строк` — asserted, never measured. Actual: **509**.

```
claimed   500     typed from memory of an earlier reading
actual    509     (Get-Content $f).Count, run afterwards
```

This file's own finding is that *a number inside a fenced block reads as measured and invites
"measured how?", while the same number in a sentence reads as known.* I put an unmeasured figure
into the one format that signals the opposite — **so the format did not protect the number, it
disguised it.** Eleventh probe error of the run, in its final sentence, of the exact class the run
documented, by the person who documented it.

The refinement that survives: **a fenced block is a claim about provenance, not a source of it.**
Putting a figure in one obliges you to have run something; it does not perform the run.

⚠️ **The thesis, from the UI session's close-out, and it is the shortest true summary of the
run:** *"The two states most worth separating turned out to be in the reporting, not the code."*

```
#389        a population gap — two sibling guards walked different route sets
/data/*     a vacuous pass — a clean zero from pages that had not rendered
#392        a verification that left no artefact
the cause   a plausible story that fitted the evidence and was false
```

None of those four is a bug in the product. Each is an **artefact that could not distinguish two
states**. The one product defect — three 18px links — *"was the easy part once the guard could see
the route."* Eight PRs shipped, and the expensive work was almost entirely in instruments and
records rather than in code.

- **The marked-guess format: 3 of 3.** Every hypothesis in every brief was refuted by
  measurement, none implemented. It did not make the briefs right; it made being wrong
  *productive*. One session: *"neither would have surfaced if the brief had just told me what to
  build."*
- **A write boundary raises read quality**, which nothing claimed. A session read a file top to
  bottom *because it could not edit it* — a finding you cannot act on must survive a handover,
  which is a higher bar than one you can quietly fix.
- **Errors live in prose.** Six wrong elapsed figures and two unit mismatches across all four
  participants — and **not one wrong number inside a fenced block**, by anyone.
- ⚠️ **And the better account of why, from the session that made one:** the errors tracked
  **whether anything depended on the number.** The same figure, in the same session, was handled
  correctly where a decision rested on it and wrongly where nothing did —
  `budget ends 09:13Z … a 1h47m shortfall` treats `11:00Z` as UTC and is right; the later aside
  `the gate is ~20 minutes away` treats it as local and is wrong by three hours. So this is not
  carelessness distributed evenly. **Attention follows consequence, and the throwaway line is
  where a wrong number lives longest** — which is also why a summary is more dangerous than the
  work it summarises.
- **Six false alarms from the orchestrator's own probes**, every one from searching a remembered
  string instead of the subject. None was caught by care; each by a control or by the result being
  implausible.
- **A correct fix can be unobservable from the wire by design.** #390 carried a discriminator
  (`ageMs` exceeding the old code's structural ceiling by 17.6×); #393 does not — both builds yield
  the same 9 rates. Production confirmed only that nothing regressed, and that is the weaker claim.
- ⚠️ **Execute the claim you are about to ship, in the commit that ships it.** A session wrote a
  comment saying *"`tests/ecbOneParser.test.ts` fails if it goes"* — a claim about behaviour — and
  then deleted the guarded line exactly as a future reader would, before shipping the sentence:

  ```
  baseline                 11 passed  0 failed
  anchor occurrences 1, applied true
  WITH THE THROW DELETED    9 passed  2 failed   both assertions NAMED
  restore byte-identical    true
  ```

  The comment now sits at the line a future reader would delete, carries the measurement that
  makes the case, and names the test that stops them. This is the *"an example in guidance is a
  claim about behaviour"* rule applied to a comment while writing it, which is the cheapest moment
  it will ever be available.

- **A verifier caught a false claim in prose sitting beside correct code** — the one defect no
  green suite can flag, and a better outcome than an approval. The shipped sentence *"one parser,
  so the green cannot outlive the ticker at any strictness"* was false: two callers read
  **different fields of the same parse**, so a shared parser removes vocabulary drift and leaves
  field drift untouched. The code was right and the **reason** was not — and the reason is what
  survives to be acted on.

- **Recusal earned its keep.** The orchestrator argued a session into that change with the
  sentence that turned out to be incomplete. Had the orchestrator also verified it, it would have
  been checking its own reasoning against itself.


- ⚠️ **THE VERIFICATION LOOP CLOSED ITSELF — and this is the evidence for the artefact rule.**
  Two writer sessions that never spoke to each other directly. The newsroom session reviewed the
  data session's #393 and left its finding as a **PR comment**, because that is the only channel
  GitHub permits here. The data session read it, acted on it, and shipped #395 — **whose title is
  the review's recommendation**:

  ```
  #393   reviews 0        <- structurally unreachable, self-approval forbidden
         comments 1       <- the entire verification channel
  #395   title "One parser removes vocabulary drift; the throw removes field drift"
  ```

  Verified independently on master, with a positive control:

  ```
  ecb.js  'at any strictness'  GONE (over-claim removed)      True
  ecb.js  'NOT sufficient' warning present                    True
  ss.js   rates-empty throw survives                          True
  POSITIVE CONTROL  parseDaily x5 in a 4553-byte file         probe demonstrably reads
  NEG CONTROL       impossible string                         False
  ```

  **A comment naming what was re-run and what it printed was readable enough for a stranger to
  act on.** That is the whole case for gate 3 requiring an artefact rather than testimony, and it
  did not need me to enforce it — the record enforced itself.

  ⚠️ **And "readable" is not the operative property — the reviewer's own qualifier, and it is the
  one that makes the rule work:**

  > *A comment saying "looks incomplete" would have died just as quietly as testimony. The channel
  > mattered; so did what went down it.*

  The artefact worked because it was **actionable without a round trip** — it carried a
  measurement, a mechanism, and **the exact line a future reader would delete**. The author was
  gone by the time it was acted on, so anything requiring a follow-up question would have been
  worth nothing.

  ```
  "looks incomplete"                     needs the author -> dies with the session
  measurement + mechanism + the line     needs nobody     -> survives and changes code
  ```

  So gate 3's requirement is not *leave a comment*. It is **leave something a stranger can execute
  after you are gone.**

- ⚠️ **A NEGATIVE CONTROL ALONE CERTIFIES NOTHING.** The reviewer nearly filed a false negative
  against its own finding. Searching `ecb.js` for the PR title's phrases:

  ```
  'vocabulary drift'  : 0
  'field drift'       : 0
  CONTROL impossible  : 0     <- INDISTINGUISHABLE from the two above
  ```

  Three zeros, and the impossible-string control **cannot separate "absent" from "the read
  failed"** — both produce 0. What settled it was a *fourth* reading: a phrase known to be there
  beforehand, returning non-zero. The phrases were in the **commit message**, not the code, which
  no amount of staring at three zeros would ever have revealed.

  This is the sibling of Track 3's other control finding — *a control that fails where it must
  pass is the only thing that reveals a vacuous subject reading*. Same family, both halves needed:

  ```
  NEGATIVE control  proves the probe can say NO      blind to a failed read
  POSITIVE control  proves the probe can say YES     the one that discriminates here
  ```

  `AGENTS.md` states the habit (*"confirm the probe can see a thing you already know is there"*).
  It does not state that a **negative** control is structurally incapable of doing that job.

  ⚠️ **The rule transferred in 20 minutes, to a different party, on a different subject, and caught
  a live error.** Checking the three run worktrees for uncommitted work, my probe returned:

  ```
  matched : 0
  CONTROL, a name that cannot exist : 0     <- INDISTINGUISHABLE
  ```

  I was one sentence from reporting *"the worktrees are already cleaned up."* Printing the
  population instead:

  ```
  samoletovs-crispy-goggles        branch samoletovs-newsroom-depth-173   dirty=False
  samoletovs-didactic-winner       branch samoletovs-ui-mobile-pass       dirty=False
  samoletovs-psychic-happiness     branch samoletovs-ecb-two-drifts       dirty=False
  ```

  **All three exist.** The directory names are randomly generated and share nothing with the branch
  names, so matching branch names against paths finds nothing — the same session→worktree mapping
  error I had already made and published once today. The conclusion (*all clean, nothing
  uncommitted*) happened to be **right**, which is the case this book says collides with nothing,
  ever.

  This is the tenth probe error of the run and the first caught by a rule rather than by a
  contradiction — because the rule arrived from a session twenty minutes earlier and was still in
  hand.

- **The gate failed at 07:56 and was working by 08:13**, repaired by two sessions independently:
  one declined a merge it was authorised to make, the other left the artefact.
- ⚠️ **Every crossed message today resolved to a default, and every default happened to be
  right.** A session merged #392 on a standing authorisation while the instruction not to was in
  flight; I told another to stop on an ambiguity it could have resolved in its own favour. Both
  defaults were the correct call — **which is luck twice, not process twice.** The fix is not more
  care: **a request for a decision needs a hold, not a default.** With ~7 crossed messages in three
  hours, a programme that relies on the default being right is running an untested branch
  constantly.
